slides.title: Reversing the decline in operating margin
Key questions

claims.claim: How can Harlow lift its operating margin from 1.0% to at least 3.0% by FY2028, within $25M of one-time cost and with at least $20M of operating income in FY2026, and which actions should come first?
evidence: Decision maker: CEO, asking the board to approve the margin plan

Success criteria: Operating margin of at least 3.0% by FY2028; Operating income of at least $20M in FY2026 (lender covenant); At most $25M of one-time cost or capital over FY2026–FY2028; Delivery kept in some form; no closure of a store with a lease beyond 2027 without a board vote
Timing: Board meeting, February 2027
Out of scope: Closing the delivery service; New stores, acquisitions and refinancing; Sales growth from new formats

slides.title: Contents
Sales grew 6% in two years, but operating income fell by more than two-thirds to $15.3M

claims.claim: Sales rose in both years, adding $83M by FY2025
Operating income fell in both years, and faster in FY2025
evidence: Operating income, $M: FY2023 47.9; FY2024 33.4; FY2025 15.3
Operating margin fell from 3.37% to 1.02% of sales over the period
Operating income fell $18.1M in FY2025 alone

slides.title: Gross margin and e-commerce, not store labor, account for nearly four-fifths of the lost operating income

claims.claim: Wages are a small part of the story: 78.8% of the $35.4M shortfall comes from gross margin and e-commerce
evidence: Bridge, $M: FY2023 47.9; Sales growth +2.8; Gross margin rate −15.3; Store labor −4.5; Occupancy and energy −3.0; E-commerce fulfillment −12.6; FY2025 15.3
Gross margin rate: down from 26.0% to 25.0% of sales, through promotions and shrink
E-commerce: fulfillment net of fees rose from 0.4% to 1.2% of sales
Store labor: 13% of the shortfall, yet it is the only line the draft plan targets
Other SG&A: unchanged at 4.7% of sales

slides.title: Reaching 3.0% by FY2028 takes about $30M more operating income a year, and the covenant needs $4.7M more in FY2026

claims.claim: $4.7M more needed in FY2026 to meet the lender's $20M covenant
evidence: FY2025: $15.3M, down $18.1M in one year
Another year like FY2025 would take operating income below zero
Must come from actions that pay inside the year

claims.claim: $29.8M more a year to reach the 3.0% target at FY2025 sales
evidence: About twice today's operating income
Fewer stores lower the dollars needed (section 5)

claims.claim: $14.5M a year: what management's 8% hours cut is expected to save
evidence: About 49% of the gap to 3.0%
Margin of 2.0% even if all of it holds
Aimed at labor, the smallest of the three causes

slides.title: Contents
Gross margin offers the largest prize, through three moves: fewer promotions, more private label and less shrink

claims.claim: Promotions grew past the point where they pay, and the events that lose money can go first
evidence: 38% of FY2025 promotional events lost money after counting the extra units sold

claims.claim: Private label earns more on every dollar and answers ValuMart on price
evidence: 12 pp more gross margin on private label than on national brands

claims.claim: Shrink follows staffing, so it falls where receiving and produce work is protected
evidence: 3.1% shrink in the least-staffed quarter of stores, against 2.3% in the best-staffed

claims.claim: Sized on the following pages, the three moves are worth about $17M a year by FY2028

slides.title: 2a: The shift to promotions was the largest drag on gross margin, about four times what private label won back

claims.claim: Promotions, not prices, drained gross margin; $10.5M a year: what the shift to promotions costs at FY2025 sales
evidence: Gross-margin effect, pp: Promotional mix −0.7; Shrink −0.5; Private-label mix +0.18
Promoted sales earn 14 percentage points less, and their share rose by 5 percentage points
Shrink: up from 2.1% to 2.6% of sales
Private label: share up from 17.0% to 18.5%, at 12 percentage points more margin
The three drivers add up to the 1.02 percentage-point fall in the gross-margin rate

slides.title: 2a: Harlow pays more for promotions on two counts: 29% of sales are now promoted, and vendors fund less of each markdown

claims.claim: One sales dollar in four was promoted in FY2023; nearly three in ten by FY2025
evidence: +5 pp
Promotional share: FY2023 24%; FY2024 26.2%; FY2025 29%

claims.claim: Harlow now pays 54% of each markdown itself, up from 45%
evidence: −9 pp
Vendor funding: FY2023 55%; FY2025 46%
Category managers raised promotional depth in FY2024–FY2025 "to defend traffic against ValuMart"

slides.title: 2a: To pay for themselves, promotions would need about 3.5% more sales, more than twice the gain the category team cites

claims.claim: Promotions would need about 3.5% more sales to pay for themselves
evidence: 5 pp more of sales on promotion × 14 pp less gross margin ÷ 20% contribution = 3.5%

claims.claim: The category team's evidence falls well short of that bar
evidence: Stores with the deepest promotions grew comparable sales 1.8% in FY2025, against 0.2% for the rest: a gap of 1.6 percentage points
That gap is a one-year correlation; it does not show that promotions caused it
Promoted sales earn less than the 20 cents a dollar used here, so the true bar is higher
41% of shoppers call Harlow more expensive, up from 33%: deeper promotions did not change price perception

slides.title: 2a: The threat promotions were meant to answer is local: stores near a new ValuMart lost 4.2% of comparable sales

claims.claim: Defend where ValuMart competes, cut elsewhere
evidence: Comparable sales FY2025: Within 3 miles of a new ValuMart −4.2%; Other Harlow stores +1.1%
11 stores have opened in Harlow trade areas since 2023
Why shoppers come: fresh produce (58%) and convenience (44%)

claims.claim: Cut loss-making events away from ValuMart first; keep targeted price investment where it competes

slides.title: 2b: Keeping private label's current pace would lift its share to about 21% by FY2028, worth about $3.8M a year

claims.claim: Private label share to about 21% by FY2028, worth $3.8M a year
evidence: Private-label share: FY2023 17%; FY2024 17.7%; FY2025 18.5%; FY2028 plan 20.75%
18.5% + 2.2 pp = 20.8%; 0.75 pp a year for 3 years
2.25 pp of sales × 12 pp margin gap × $1,412M sales

claims.claim: The value answer that also pays
evidence: each dollar moved from national brands earns 12 cents more gross margin
an own-brand price ladder answers the 41% who find Harlow expensive

slides.title: 2c: Shrink rises as staffing thins: the least-staffed stores lose 3.1% of sales, against 2.3% in the best-staffed

claims.claim: Thin staffing shows up as waste
evidence: Q1: store managers say produce rotation and receiving checks are skipped on busy days
Q3 to Q4: the extra hours buy only 0.1 percentage points less shrink
fresh and produce waste is 45% of shrink and receiving errors 20%
shrink rose from 2.1% to 2.6% of sales as hours per $1,000 of sales fell 6.0%

slides.title: 2c: Bringing the two least-staffed quarters of stores to the third quarter's shrink would save about $3.5M a year

claims.claim: Saving about $3.5M a year
evidence: 1 pp excess shrink (Q1 0.7 pp, Q2 0.3 pp) × 25% of chain sales × $1,411.9M = $3.5M

claims.claim: Hours move between stores; they are not added
evidence: Hours come from Q4 stores
Theft, 35% of shrink, is assumed unchanged
Chain shrink would fall from 2.6% to about 2.4%, still above FY2023's 2.1%

slides.title: Contents
Store costs should be reshaped rather than cut, by redeploying hours and exiting the weakest stores as leases end

claims.claim: An 8% hours cut targets the smallest cause, and much of its saving would come back as shrink
evidence: 12.7% of the operating-income shortfall since FY2023 came from store labor

claims.claim: Six of the nine loss-making stores can close at lease end, with no board vote needed
evidence: 6 of the nine stores with negative four-wall EBITDA have leases ending by 2027

slides.title: 3a: Wages are not the main cause: fewer hours absorbed most of a 9% pay rise, and labor rose 0.3 percentage points

claims.claim: Fewer hours per sales dollar offset nearly three-quarters of the wage rise
evidence: 9.4% rise in average hourly wage: $16.80 to $18.38
−5.98% labor hours per $1,000 of sales: 7.02 to 6.60
0.3 pp rise in store labor: 11.8% to 12.1% of sales
Total hours roughly flat while sales grew 6%

claims.claim: The 2027 minimum-wage rise of 4% needs the same productivity again

slides.title: 3a: An 8% hours cut could give back up to $10M of its $14.5M saving through higher shrink

claims.claim: Net saving of $4.5M before any lost sales
evidence: $14.5M: 8% of $181.9M of store labor − $10.05M extra shrink = $4.5M
hours per $1,000 of sales fell 6.0% and shrink rose 0.5 pp, about 0.08 for each 1% fewer hours
An 8% cut would add about 0.67 pp of shrink on FY2025 sales of $1,503M

claims.claim: Even if all of the $14.5M held, the margin would reach only about 2.0%

slides.title: 3b: Nine stores lose money at the four-wall level, and six can go without a board vote as leases end

claims.claim: Nine stores lose money at the four-wall level
evidence: 9 of 58 stores had negative four-wall EBITDA
$118M combined sales, 7.9% of chain sales, four-wall EBITDA loss of $3.1M
25% of the sales would move to nearby Harlow stores, as in past closures

claims.claim: Letting the six leases run out costs nothing and needs no board vote
evidence: 6 of the nine have leases ending by 2027
The other three need a vote and $7.5M to exit

slides.title: 3b: Exiting the nine stores would add about $6.6M a year, and the six with expiring leases need no board vote

claims.claim: Exiting all nine adds $6.6M a year
Six exits need no board vote; the other three cost $7.5M
evidence: The six add about $4.4M a year
The other three add about $2.2M a year for a one-time $7.5M, a payback of about 3.4 years
Chain sales fall by about $88.5M

slides.title: Contents
E-commerce can keep its delivery service, but only if delivery stops being subsidized

claims.claim: Counted in full, e-commerce loses money; the reported profit leaves out delivery and counts every sale as new
evidence: 30% of online spend is new to Harlow

claims.claim: Home delivery, not click-and-collect, causes most of the loss
evidence: $10.7 per delivered order: third-party delivery cost minus the fee collected

claims.claim: Repricing delivery as tested recovers part of the loss and keeps the service
evidence: $6.4 average fee per delivered order in the fee test, against $3.10 today

slides.title: 4a: E-commerce fulfillment cost more than tripled in two years, to $18.1M, the fastest-rising cost Harlow has

claims.claim: Growth came with the costliest kind of order
evidence: Fulfillment cost, $M: FY2023 5.2; FY2024 10.9; FY2025 18.1
Orders: 2.9 times as many as in FY2023, basket about $96
Home delivery: up from 45% to 58% of orders
Gap per delivery widened from $9.50 to $10.70
Fulfillment cost per dollar of e-commerce sales, FY2025: 14.2%
E-commerce rose from 3.0% to 8.5% of sales

slides.title: 4a: Counted in full, e-commerce loses about $10M a year, because its new sales cover less than half of fulfillment

claims.claim: E-commerce contribution after fulfillment is −$10.4M
evidence: 70% would have been spent in its stores (survey, n = 2,300)
New sales cover 42% of fulfillment; home delivery carries about nine-tenths of the loss

claims.claim: Where data is missing, the estimate favors e-commerce
evidence: Store costs saved when an existing customer shops online are not counted
The 30% comes from customers' own answers and could be lower
Packaging and technology costs outside the fulfillment line are not counted

slides.title: 4a: The team's 6.1% profit comes from leaving out delivery and counting every online sale as new

claims.claim: The team's 6.1% profit comes from leaving out delivery and counting every online sale as new
evidence: Sales counted: team all sales as new vs only the 30% new — largest correction
Third-party delivery: left out vs included net of fees, $8.3M net in FY2025
Result FY2025: 6.1% (about $7.8M) vs a loss of about $10.4M, 8% of e-commerce sales — a swing of nearly $18M

slides.title: 4b: Each home delivery loses about $12, more than seven times the loss on a click-and-collect order

claims.claim: Delivery, not online shopping, is the problem
evidence: Per delivered order: contribution $5.76; picking −$7.4; third-party delivery −$13.8; fee +$3.1; result −$12.34
7.5x the loss on a click-and-collect order
Click-and-collect: loses about $1.64 an order
Delivered orders: 58% of orders but about nine-tenths of the e-commerce loss

slides.title: 4c: Customers accept a higher delivery fee: the test doubled the fee per delivery while e-commerce sales fell only 2%

claims.claim: Customers accept a higher delivery fee
evidence: Test: 4 stores, 10 weeks, late FY2025: fee $7.99, free delivery from $100
$6.4 average fee per delivered order, up from $3.10 (2.1 times)
−9% delivered orders
+14% click-and-collect orders
−2% total e-commerce sales
Only 4 stores for 10 weeks: confirm in the rollout

claims.claim: Delivery stays, priced closer to what it costs

slides.title: 4c: Rolled out to every store, the tested fee would cut the e-commerce loss by about $2.8M a year

claims.claim: Tested fee chain-wide gains $2.8M a year
evidence: Costs per order stay at FY2025 levels: $7.40 to pick, $13.80 to deliver

claims.claim: The fee is a first step; the delivery contract matters as much
evidence: Every $1 off the delivery rate at renewal adds about $0.7M a year; the proposed 3% rise would cost about $0.3M
E-commerce would still lose about $7.6M a year

slides.title: Contents
Together the actions would lift operating income from $15.3M to about $42M a year by FY2028

One-time cost: $7.5M to exit three leases, within the $25M limit
Store labor held at 12.1% of sales

claims.claim: Operating margin returns to about 3.0% with almost no cushion

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: Adopt the recommended plan instead of management's 8% hours cut: cut loss-making promotions (away from ValuMart first, back to 24% of sales), grow private label, move hours to receiving and produce to cut shrink, roll out the tested delivery fee and re-tender the delivery contract, and exit the nine loss-making stores (six as leases end, three after a board vote). "Approve the promotion reset and the fee now; the store vote and private label follow."

alternatives_considered.option: Management's draft: cut hours 8%, freeze e-commerce
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: about 2.0% margin if the full $14.5M holds, nearer 1.3% if shrink rises; up to $10M of the saving could come back as shrink; risks fresh produce and checkout staffing. "Only the plan reaches the target."
Left out: it held at 4.7% of sales in FY2023–25, so it did not cause the decline
Left out (and out of scope): the family owners want delivery kept; repricing it is the route
Left out: deeper promotions already lost margin and did not change price perception
Left out: 41% of shoppers already call Harlow more expensive, up from 33%

alternatives_considered.option: Exiting the three stores whose leases run beyond 2027
alternatives_considered.treatment: Included subject to a board vote: adds about $2.2M a year for $7.5M, payback about 3.4 years; keeping them lowers FY2028 margin to about 2.76%

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Eight planning assumptions for the CEO and CFO to confirm: promotions 24%, private-label gain 0.8 pp a year, Q1/Q2 shrink 2.4%, 25% sales per store quarter, 30% online spend new, 20% contribution per new dollar, 25% sales kept from closed stores, 66.7% store gain from six leases
Planning assumptions chosen in this review (user unavailable to confirm)
All lever sizes use FY2025 prices, volumes and cost rates; the 3.0% target is measured on the sales left after the store exits and the fee change
The plan is about $0.4M short of 3.0%, with almost no cushion; it needs the 2027 wage rise absorbed (otherwise about 2.5%)
The 1.6 pp comp gap for deep-promotion stores is a one-year correlation; it does not show that promotions caused it
The briefing pack does not give the number of Harlow stores within three miles of a ValuMart
Shrink saving treats the pattern across store quarters as cause and effect; Q4 shrink may rise a little as hours leave; theft assumed unchanged
Hours-cut shrink estimate is an upper bound attributing the whole FY2023–25 shrink rise to thinner staffing; lost sales not counted
E-commerce estimate: store costs saved, packaging and technology costs not counted; the 30% new spend comes from customers' own answers and could be lower
Fee test covered only 4 stores for 10 weeks: confirm in the rollout
Store-exit gain uses four-wall EBITDA as a stand-in; depreciation saved not counted; gain split evenly by store
Covenant holds only if the FY2025 slide stops; a repeat of the $18.1M fall would breach it
Confirm the covenant test period with the CFO; if FY2026 ends January 2027, most of it has passed by the board meeting
Vendor funding for FY2024 is not in the briefing pack
FY2024 operating income is reported as $33.4M although the lines sum to $33.3M
Wage-rise hours estimate is an upper bound assuming the 4% rise lifts every wage
Largest risk: loss of traffic to ValuMart when promotions are cut; also delivery demand, delivery contract 3% rise, and less than 25% sales transfer from closed stores
next_steps: Start the promotion reset: stop repeating loss-making events, beginning away from ValuMart — Chief merchant — Now
Roll out the tested $7.99 delivery fee and $100 free-delivery threshold to every store — E-commerce lead — Within a month
Re-tender the delivery contract and confirm with the lender which months the FY2026 covenant covers — CFO — Now, before renewal
Replace the 8% hours cut with a move of hours to receiving and produce in Q1 and Q2 stores — COO — First quarter
Let the six leases lapse and put the other three exits to a board vote — CEO with the board — February 2027 board
normalized.extraction_notes: The deck has no images; every chart came through as series data. Chart values given as fractions (for example 0.29) are shown here as percentages. Chart values in waterfall and bridge charts are rounded from the extracted series. Executive-summary sub-bullets are listed as separate entries with a leading dash. The governing thought is the headline of the executive summary.
